doc_name: Pakistan men's national field hockey team
text: The Pakistan men's national field hockey team, known as the Green Shirts, represents Pakistan in international field hockey and has been administered by the Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) since its establishment in 1948. The team played its first international match in 1948, defeating Belgium 2–1 at the London Olympics, where it remained unbeaten in the group stage, defeating the Netherlands 6–1 and later winning fourth place. The PHF was a founding member of the Asian Hockey Federation (ASHF) formed in 1958 and has been a member of the International Hockey Federation (FIH) since 1948. Pakistan is one of the most successful national field hockey teams globally, with four Hockey World Cup victories in 1971, 1978, 1982, and 1994, and has won eight gold medals at the Asian Games in 1958, 1962, 1970, 1974, 1978, 1982, 1990, and 2010. It is the only Asian team to have won the Champions Trophy three times (1978, 1980, 1994) and has won a total of 29 official international titles, including three Olympic gold medals in Rome 1960, Mexico City 1968, and Los Angeles 1984. The team has been ranked world number one by the FIH in both 2000 and 2001. Former captain Sohail Abbas holds the second-highest total of international goals in field hockey history, while Waseem Ahmad is the most-capped player with 410 appearances between 1996 and 2013. Field hockey is the national sport of Pakistan. The team has a fierce rivalry with India, having played each other in 20 major tournament finals, winning 13 titles, and consecutively winning the first three Hockey Asia Cup championships in 1982, 1985, and 1989. Notable rivalries also exist with the Netherlands and Australia. The team's home ground is the National Hockey Stadium in Lahore, with current head coach Shahnaz Sheikh and team manager Saeed Khan. The game was introduced to British India by British servicemen and became popular, with players from pre-partition India representing Pakistan after 1947. The PHF established provincial associations in West Punjab, East Bengal, Sindh, Balochistan, Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, Bahawalpur, and Services. Pakistan won its first Olympic medal in 1956, earning silver in Melbourne by losing to India 1–0. At the 1958 Asian Games in Tokyo, Pakistan won its first gold medal by finishing top of the group after drawing 0–0 with India. In 1960, Pakistan won gold at the Rome Olympics by defeating India 1–0 in the final, with Naseer Bunda scoring the goal. In 1962, Pakistan won its second Asian Games gold medal under captain Chaudhry Ghulam Rasool. In 1964, Pakistan finished as runners-up in the Tokyo Olympics and in the 1966 Asian Games in Bangkok. In 1968, Pakistan won its second Olympic gold medal by defeating Australia 2–1, with goals from Muhammad Asad Malik and Abdul Rashid, who scored seven goals and was the top scorer. In 1970, Pakistan won its third Asian Games gold by defeating India 1–0 in the final. In 1971, the first Hockey World Cup was scheduled in Pakistan but was moved to Barcelona due to political tensions between Pakistan and India during the Bangladesh Liberation War, with Pakistan's ambassador H.E. Masood formally handing over the trophy in Brussels. Pakistan won the first Hockey World Cup in 1971 by defeating India 1–0 in the final, with Tanvir Dar scoring eight goals and becoming the top scorer. In 1972, Pakistan finished fourth at the Munich Olympics, losing to West Germany 1–0. In 1973, Pakistan lost the Hockey World Cup to India. In 1974, Pakistan won the Asian Games and retained its title in 1975, losing to India in the World Cup final. In 1976, Pakistan won its first bronze medal at the Montreal Olympics. In 1978, Pakistan won three major tournaments: the third Hockey World Cup in Buenos Aires, the 1978 Asian Games, and the first Champions Trophy. In 1980, Pakistan boycotted the Moscow Olympics due to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, and hosted the Champions Trophy in 1980 and 1981, winning the title against West Germany in 1980. In the 1980s, Pakistan won every tournament it participated in, including the 1982 World Cup in Mumbai and the 1984 Olympics in Los Angeles, defeating West Germany in the final. Pakistan also won the Asian Games and Asia Cup consecutively during this period. From the 1970s, hockey was played on synthetic surfaces, and the FIH fully transitioned to AstroTurf in 1986, which changed the game's pace and focus to strength and speed, negatively affecting Pakistan due to limited access to synthetic pitches compared to European nations. Pakistan finished 11th at the 1986 World Cup, winning only one pool game. The team later regained dominance, finishing runner-up at the 1990 World Cup in Lahore and winning a bronze medal at the 1992 Olympics in Barcelona. In 1994, Pakistan won the Champions Trophy at home and the Hockey World Cup in Sydney after defeating the Netherlands in a penalty shootout. After the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, Pakistan finished fifth at the 1998 World Cup in Utrecht, won the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup in 1999, finished fourth at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, and won a bronze medal at the 2002 Champions Trophy. At the 2002 Asian Games, Pakistan finished fourth, its first time without a medal. In 2003, Pakistan lost the Asia Cup final to India. In 2004, Pakistan finished fifth at the Athens Olympics and third at the Champions Trophy in Lahore, securing a third consecutive bronze. In 2005, Pakistan defeated Olympic champion Australia to win the Hockey RaboTrophy in the Netherlands. In 2006, Pakistan finished sixth at the World Cup and failed to progress from the pool stages of the 2007 Asia Cup. In 2008, Pakistan finished eighth at the Beijing Olympics. In 2010, the team finished last at the World Cup in New Delhi (12th) but won gold at the Asian Games in China. In 2011, Pakistan finished seventh at the Olympics and won bronze at the 2012 Champions Trophy in Melbourne, defeating favorites like Germany. The team's most successful tournament during this period was winning the Asian Hockey Champions Trophy in 2012 against India and finishing as runners-up in 2011. Despite no major team honors, the team featured world-renowned individual players such as Sohail Abbas, who scored 348 goals and was top scorer at the 2002 World Cup and 2004 Olympics, and Rehan Butt, who was twice voted Best Asian Player by the Asian Hockey Federation, along with Shakeel Abbasi, Salman Akbar, and Muhammad Saqlain. Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2014 World Cup after finishing third in the 2013 Asia Cup, and failed to qualify for the Olympics for the first time at Rio 2016 after losing in the 2014–15 FIH Hockey World League qualifiers. From 2016 to 2017, Pakistan performed poorly, including a record 9–1 defeat against Australia in 2017. In 2018, Roelant Oltmans was appointed coach, showing some improvement but failing to win a match at the 2018 World Cup. Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics after losing the Olympic qualifiers to the Netherlands in a two-legged tie in 2019. The PHF announced Pakistan's participation in the 2021 Asian Champions Trophy, its first international competition after a two-year gap, with a 20-man squad and Siegfried Aikman as head coach. Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2023 World Cup despite it being a 16-team event. Pakistan participated in the 2022 Commonwealth Games, finishing seventh, and in the 2022 Nations Cup, also finishing seventh. In July 2023, Shahnaz Sheikh was appointed head coach for the 2023 Asian Champions Trophy, and in August 2023, a 36-man squad was announced for the Asian Games 2023. At the 2023 Asian Games, Pakistan lost to India 10–2, the worst defeat in its history, finishing fifth. Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2024 Summer Olympics. In 2024, Roelant Oltmans was brought in as coach for the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup and the Nations Cup. In July 2025, Pakistan's under-18 team lost 3–0 to Japan in the Men's U-18 Asia Cup final at the National Hockey Training Centre, highlighting a systemic decline attributed to government neglect, lack of investment in grassroots development, and poor institutional support. Critics argue such defeats reflect a broader national apathy toward sports excellence. Pakistan received an invitation from the FIH to compete in the 2025–26 FIH Pro League, qualifying for the tournament. The team's official motif features a star and crescent on a dark green field with a vertical white stripe at the hoist, matching the colors of the Pakistani flag.

doc_name: Pakistan men's national field hockey team
text: Pakistan failed to qualify for the 2024 Summer Olympics. In 2024, Roelant Oltmans was appointed as the coach of Pakistan for the Sultan Azlan Shah Cup and the Nations Cup. In July 2025, Pakistan's under-18 men's team lost 3–0 to Japan in the final of the Men's U-18 Asia Cup, held at the National Hockey Training Centre. Despite showing early aggression and taking multiple penalty corners, Pakistan failed to convert key opportunities, highlighting a systemic decline in the sport due to chronic government neglect, lack of investment in grassroots development, and poor institutional support. Critics argue that such defeats reflect a broader national apathy toward sports excellence. Pakistan received an invitation from the FIH to compete in the 2025–26 FIH Pro League, thereby qualifying for the tournament. The official motif of the Pakistan national field hockey team features a star and crescent on a dark green field, with a vertical white stripe at the hoist, matching the colors of Pakistan's national flag. Pakistan has played matches at various venues across the country, but by 1978, the primary venue became the National Hockey Stadium in Lahore—also known as Gaddafi Hockey Stadium, named after former Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi—considered the largest international field hockey stadium in the world with a capacity of 45,000 spectators. The Pakistan Hockey Federation (PHF) is headquartered at this stadium. Pakistan has hosted numerous international events, including the Hockey Asia Cup in 1982 and the Champions Trophy in 1978, 1980, 1981, 1983, 1984, 1986, 1988, 1992, 1994, 1998, and 2004, as well as the 1990 Hockey World Cup, where Pakistan lost 3–1 to the Netherlands in the final. Since its debut at the 1948 Summer Olympics, Pakistan has won more than 20 official titles. As of 27 October 2019, players in bold are still active with the national team. Eighteen players were named in the squad for the 2024 Men's Asian Champions Trophy in Hulunbuir. Caps and goals are current as of 9 June 2024, following the match against South Africa. All times are in (UTC+5). Pakistan participated in the 2024–25 Men's FIH Hockey Nations Cup, the 2025 Asia Play-offs, and the 2025–26 Men's FIH Pro League. The record was last updated following Pakistan's match against Argentina at Santiago del Estero, Argentina, in the 2025–26 Men's FIH Pro League on 15 December 2025.
